# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **Black Hills will build 564 megawatts of gas in Cheyenne for Google's data centre.**

**What You Need to Know:** Black Hills will build 564 megawatts of gas-fired generation in Cheyenne, Wyoming, for Google's planned data centre, inside a resource mix it puts at about 2.7 gigawatts. Samsung's high-bandwidth memory share is reported at 33 percent, and GlobalFoundries has unveiled an FD-SOI platform aimed at machines that sense and act rather than at data-centre GPUs. A council in northern Italy has rejected an 80-megawatt data centre.

### Top Story
Black Hills Corp., the South Dakota-based utility holding company, has announced 564 megawatts of new natural-gas generation at its existing Cheyenne Prairie Generating Station in Cheyenne, Wyoming, to serve Google's planned data-centre load, with the units to be built between 2027 and 2029. Power Engineering reports the new capacity would cost 1.8 billion dollars and would be owned by a non-regulated Black Hills affiliate, not the Wyoming utility. Black Hills would manage about 2.1 gigawatts of third-party resources — the project release suggests turbines and fuel cells — on a privately managed microgrid under Wyoming's Large Power Contract Service tariff, taking a management fee rather than owning those assets. The company said the project would draw on a total resource mix of about 2.7 gigawatts, including reserve margins and excluding transmission expansion. Google would cover the cost of serving the data centre, with contractual protections on stranded assets, early termination and unexpected costs intended to shield existing utility customers, and has advanced 399 million dollars for long-lead equipment that Black Hills expects to reimburse before July 2027. Black Hills projects about 150 million dollars of net income from the project in 2030 and 2.4 billion dollars of unlevered free cash flow through 2048, has secured an air-quality permit for the Cheyenne Prairie expansion, and is pursuing additional siting and transmission approvals. Source: [power-eng.com](https://www.power-eng.com/onsite-power/microgrids/google-wyoming-data-center-black-hills-natural-gas/)

### Silicon
**Samsung's HBM Market Share Jumps to 33%; Hybrid Bonding Technology Could Be Key to Overtaking Rivals: BigGo Finance**
BigGo Finance reports Samsung's high-bandwidth memory market share at 33 percent, drawing on an expert interview published by Damnang Research on October 6. The September 19 interview was with a process-development engineer at SK Hynix's Future Technology Research Institute; the notes say the remarks are personal views, not the company's position, and the full transcript is behind a paywall. That interviewee said SK Hynix is having difficulty developing hybrid bonding for next-generation HBM, while Samsung is reportedly already delivering samples that use the technology. On June 18, SK Hynix said it had delivered 12-layer HBM4E samples of 48 gigabytes to major customers on its existing Advanced MR-MUF packaging, with a 17 percent improvement in thermal resistance compared with HBM4. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/8cf13cfd-eeeb-4d5f-9529-f744b979d76a)

**Manfred Horstmann: GlobalFoundries Bets on FDX Fusion for Physical AI: EE Times**
EE Times reports that GlobalFoundries on October 9 unveiled FDX Fusion in Dresden, a strained-silicon fully depleted silicon-on-insulator platform it says can deliver 7-nanometre-class digital performance without extreme ultraviolet lithography, at more than twice the density of its first-generation FDX, and that combines RF, analog, mixed-signal, embedded nonvolatile memory, in-memory computing and dense logic. Manfred Horstmann, senior vice president and general manager of European fabs, told EE Times that data-centre AI is extremely power hungry, and that physical AI needs sensors, actuators, communications, low power and cost efficiency — what GlobalFoundries calls STAC, for sense, think, act, communicate. GlobalFoundries expects to invest roughly 1 billion dollars over the coming years in FDX Fusion development, including about 250 million dollars for the initial capability toolset. The transistor channel sits in an approximately 70-angstrom, or 7-nanometre, silicon film above a buried oxide, thin enough that the channel is inherently fully depleted. The same day the company marked the topping-off of SPRINT, its Dresden fab expansion supported under the European Chips Act, adding cleanroom, laboratory and manufacturing capacity. Semiconductor Digest carried the same roadmap. Source: [eetimes.com](https://www.eetimes.com/manfred-horstmann-globalfoundries-bets-on-fdx-fusion-for-physical-ai/)
https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/gf-unveils-roadmap-to-deliver-the-worlds-most-advanced-fd-soi-platform-for-physical-ai/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=gf-unveils-roadmap-to-deliver-the-worlds-most-advanced-fd-soi-platform-for-physical-ai

**Microchip Technology Acquires VORAGO Technologies: Semiconductor Digest**
Semiconductor Digest reports that Microchip Technology has acquired VORAGO Technologies, a privately held Austin, Texas supplier of radiation-hardened and radiation-tolerant microcontrollers and microprocessors. Microchip described the purchase as done and described itself as a broadline semiconductor supplier. Source: [semiconductor-digest.com](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/microchip-technology-acquires-vorago-technologies/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=microchip-technology-acquires-vorago-technologies)

### Data Centres & Power
**Council rejects 80MW data center in northern Italy: Data Center Dynamics**
Data Center Dynamics reports that a council in northern Italy has rejected an 80-megawatt data centre. The municipality argues the plans go against its environmental policy. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/council-rejects-80mw-data-center-in-northern-italy/)

**Speed Bumps Slow Asia-Pacific's Data Center Gold Rush: Data Center Knowledge**
Data Center Knowledge reports that Firmus and PLDT pulled data-centre initial public offerings this week. Governments in the region pressed pause on development. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/investing/speed-bumps-slow-asia-pacific-s-data-center-gold-rush)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**Fermilab to Lead 2 New Genesis Mission Awards: HPCwire**
HPCwire reports that on October 9, 2026, Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory received two new awards under the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission. The awards expand Fermilab's role by developing custom microelectronics and advancing quantum information science. The Genesis Mission is described as a national effort to double productivity and overall impact. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/fermilab-to-lead-2-new-genesis-mission-awards/)

### The Teardown: When the Module Price Is the Allocation
A finished memory module does not record whether its die was bid against an accelerator. The choice is made at wafer start and in the back-end that turns a die into something a board can accept. High-bandwidth parts take advanced DRAM, stacking and test time. Ordinary DRAM and NAND still need cleanroom hours, probe capacity, substrates and module assembly from an industry already steering people and tools toward the higher-margin AI package. When that shared capacity tightens, the line that used to be a small item on a bill of materials becomes the line that sets the shelf price.

TechPowerUp, reporting Circana figures that analyst Mat Piscatella shared on Bluesky, measured the US console market for 2026 through August. Xbox hardware unit sales were down 33 percent from a year earlier. The average price paid for a new Xbox was 529 dollars. A new PlayStation averaged 597 dollars. Total hardware unit sales in August were 559,000, the lowest August total since 2013. Piscatella tied the slump to price hikes that followed the memory and storage shortage.

The mechanism is a queue. A fab books a wafer start well ahead of the shelf. A start aimed at a stacked DRAM die does not later become a console chip. A start that is standard DRAM or NAND still competes for testers, engineers and often the same substrate vendors the AI package is already loading. The device maker then meets two constraints at once: a higher contract price, and a shipment slot that can slip after that price is accepted. Unit sales fall when either constraint binds. The average selling price in the Circana data is what remains after the buyer who would not pay has already left the sample.

That pass-through stops clearing the market when the missing constraint is no longer price. If the module is simply not on the line — testers full, substrates late, NAND held for data-centre drives — a discount does not create a unit. Availability, not the sticker, is what then decides whether a launch weekend ships.

### On the Horizon
- Demonstrator silicon for GlobalFoundries' FDX Fusion is targeted for early 2027, with an initial process design kit planned for mid-2027.
- Black Hills expects to start earning returns on the Cheyenne project next year by introducing microgrid management fees.
- Black Hills expects to reimburse Google's 399 million dollar long-lead advance before July 2027, with the new gas units scheduled for 2027 through 2029.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **A two-billion-dollar pact puts US-made AI interposers into TSMC's CoWoS flow.**

**What You Need to Know:** GlobalFoundries has signed a $2 billion agreement to supply TSMC with silicon interposers from Malta, New York, for CoWoS packaging. Volume production there is scheduled for the first half of 2028 under an initial five-year contract. Elsewhere, a bankrupt Texas campus is being recast as a 73 MW research and AI compute plan, and a new coldplate claims a further cut in GPU hotspot temperature.

### Top Story
GlobalFoundries has signed a $2 billion agreement to supply TSMC with U.S.-made silicon interposers for Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate packaging, Industrial Info reports, and Electronics For You describes the same pact as a reached agreement with an initial five-year term. Capacity is to be added at GlobalFoundries' fab in Malta, New York, and the company will expand that campus. Electronics For You calls the setup the first domestic U.S. source of silicon interposers and says the parts integrate embedded deep trench capacitors to improve thermal and power efficiency in high-performance computing and AI accelerators. Volume production and the capacity ramp at the New York site are scheduled to begin in the first half of 2028, with provisions to scale further as hyperscale demand for chiplet packaging grows. Source: [industrialinfo.com](https://www.industrialinfo.com/news/article/globalfoundries-reaches-supply-agreement-with-tsmc-for-ai-chip-component--363473) | https://www.electronicsforyou.biz/industry-buzz/globalfoundries-and-tsmc-partner-on-us-interposer-production-for-cowos/ | https://finance.yahoo.com/news/globalfoundries-tsmc-agree-2bn-us-073550034.html

### Silicon
**Xsight Labs Adds E1L to DPU Portfolio with Support for up to 200G: HPCwire**
Xsight Labs announced the E1L on October 8, 2026, as the newest member of its E-Series data processing unit portfolio, HPCwire reports. The part is Arm-based and is described as delivering full DPU offload from 25 watts, with support for up to 200G in the source's own unit. It runs the same open software as the 800G E1. The announcement was issued from San Jose and Tel Aviv. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/xsight-labs-adds-e1l-to-dpu-portfolio-with-support-for-up-to-200g/)

**Intel's Packaging Technology Gains Nvidia's Interest, Easing Pressure on TSMC's Backend Operations: BigGo Finance**
This is a reported evaluation, not a confirmed Nvidia award. BigGo Finance says GF Securities analyst Jeff Pu wrote that Nvidia could adopt Intel's Foveros packaging for backend work on select AI chips in the second half of 2028, alongside an expectation that Intel's 14A process enters mass production in that same half. The piece notes a January DigiTimes report that Nvidia might use Intel 18A or 14A for next-generation GPUs. It also says Intel's EMIB and EMIB-T packaging have reportedly drawn Google for TPU chips. Foveros, as described there, stacks compute dies or chiplets on a base die rather than placing them side by side as in EMIB, which the report says shrinks horizontal footprint and improves power efficiency and data transfer speed. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/a75adb64-9283-4678-9e40-abf34eb6e9fb)

### Data Centres & Power
**ThisWay Global to Convert Bankrupt RELLIS Site into 73 MW AI Hub: Data Center Knowledge**
ThisWay Global has announced a 73 MW Research and AI Compute Center in Bryan, Texas, on Texas A&M's RELLIS Campus. Data Center Knowledge reports that a private developer began a data center there in 2024 and filed for Chapter 11 in November 2025, leaving the project unfinished, after the Texas A&M University System had explored a data center on the campus since 2013. ThisWay, an Austin company, says it acquired the project out of bankruptcy and completed the transaction on September 30, 2026. The phased plan totals 73 MW on about 25 acres of university-system land, and chief executive Stephan Fabel said the first building will encompass about 25 percent of the campus's total compute power. Capital came with Texas-based Centaurus Capital and Skylar Capital Management, among other investors, and ThisWay says that capital was to purchase the project and make creditors whole. The company plans to adjust the existing design and expand capacity, including a redesign aimed at HPC density and liquid cooling, and it intends to use the site to demonstrate a Sovereign AI Blueprint it introduced in September 2026. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/ai-data-centers/thisway-global-to-convert-bankrupt-rellis-site-into-73-mw-ai-hub)

**Frore Systems Announces New LiquidJet Diamond Coldplates for AI Factories: TechPowerUp**
Frore Systems announced LiquidJet Diamond, a liquid-cooling coldplate for AI factories with an integrated diamond spreader. The company says it boosts AI tokens per watt, and revenue, by 35 percent versus traditional skived coldplates, with that revenue increase flowing to profit. It builds on the previously announced LiquidJet coldplate, a 3D ultra-short-loop multi-stage design Frore says can be customized to each GPU power map, including extreme hotspots. Frore says LiquidJet alone cuts GPU die temperature by 12 degrees Celsius and raises tokens per watt by 25 percent. LiquidJet Diamond adds a spreader with integrated diamond wafers at the hotspot locations and, Frore says, cuts hotspot die temperature by a further 10 degrees Celsius, taking the tokens-per-watt gain to 35 percent. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/353544/frore-systems-announces-new-liquidjet-diamond-coldplates-for-ai-factories)

**CoreWeave CEO on Fox Business: Expanding to India with AdaniConneX: CoreWeave**
CoreWeave has announced a first presence in India with AdaniConneX, including a Mumbai build discussed by chief executive Michael Intrator on Fox Business. The company said it will deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin, open a local office, and hire on the ground. Intrator framed the move as customers scaling AI globally and CoreWeave going where that compute is needed. The post presents this as intent and an interview, not as an energized site. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/CoreWeave/status/2108243477444358640)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**Memory Stocks Rebound Across the Board as Micron, SanDisk and SK Hynix Gain Over 2%: TradingKey**
After a broad memory-stock decline, TradingKey reports that news of Toshiba capacity-expansion plans, also referred to in the piece as Toshiba/Kioxia, triggered fears of legacy DRAM and NAND oversupply. Cantor Fitzgerald and Mirae Asset said fears of capacity excess and of HBM price cuts were overblown. The piece says structural demand for high-capacity DDR5, enterprise SSDs, and HBM tied to AI computing buildouts remains robust, while warning that the stocks' high-beta character still leaves them open to sharp swings on short-term news. Source: [tradingkey.com](https://www.tradingkey.com/analysis/stocks/us-stocks/262208203-stock-micron-sandisk-skhynix-mu-skhy-sndk-wdc-stx-dram-nand-ssd-hbm-tradingkey)

**ORNL Selected for 6 Phase II Genesis Mission Awards: HPCwire**
On October 8, 2026, the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory was selected for six Phase II Genesis Mission awards, HPCwire reports, covering materials science, microelectronics, quantum computing, accelerator operations, HPC software development, and fusion energy. The same day's notices say Berkeley Lab will lead the Multi-Office Accelerator Team Core Project, applying AI to particle-accelerator design, and that Argonne won a further Phase II round with collaborators on software, materials, and physics. The write-ups describe significant or new funding without stating dollar amounts. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/ornl-selected-for-6-phase-ii-genesis-mission-awards/) | https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/berkeley-lab-artificial-intelligence-for-particle-accelerators-gets-another-boost/ | https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/argonne-to-advance-scientific-discovery-with-new-genesis-mission-awards/

### The Teardown: The Quarter the Channel Already Bought
A memory-price hike empties the next quarter's order book before it empties the warehouse. Vendors and distributors who can see DRAM and NAND costs rising fill the channel while the old invoice still clears. Units that end customers would have taken later leave in the first half instead. The second half then inherits stock that is already on the floor and a thinner book of new builds.

TechPowerUp, citing preliminary IDC data, puts worldwide PC shipments at 62.7 million units in the third quarter of 2026, down 20.1 percent from 78.5 million a year earlier. Shipments also fell 9.1 percent from the second quarter, even though the third quarter is normally the larger one. IDC's account, as that report carries it, is that the first half stocked up ahead of memory-driven price hikes, supply stayed constrained, and prices stayed high, so the third quarter had little demand left to work with.

The mechanism is timing, not a sudden disappearance of uses for a PC. A machine already sitting at a distributor does not get ordered again when the next invoice jumps. The OEM cuts the build plan. The memory supplier can still read the earlier pull as demand. AI server builds bidding for high-capacity DRAM and NAND are what tightened that market; the client PC is where the squeeze shows up as a missing shipment rather than as a delayed training job. The module that went to a server DIMM or an enterprise SSD is not on the notebook line, and an empty channel does not create a second source of client parts.

That forward buy stops being the right move once the pre-bought stock has cleared and the next quarter's shipments are limited by what end buyers will pay at the new memory price, not by what the channel already absorbed. Until that clearance, a steep year-on-year drop measures a timing shift as much as it measures destroyed demand. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/353538/pc-shipments-drop-20-1-in-q3-2026-hp-and-dell-hit-hardest)

### On the Horizon
- First half of 2028: GlobalFoundries schedules volume production and the capacity ramp of silicon interposers for TSMC at Malta, New York.
- Second half of 2028: Intel's 14A process is expected to enter mass production, the window in which Jeff Pu says Nvidia could adopt Foveros on select AI chips.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **Eighty billion dollars is Samsung's estimated quarter, topping Nvidia's last operating profit.**

**What You Need to Know:** Samsung Electronics estimated third-quarter operating profit at 107.4 trillion won, or $80.2 billion, a figure Euronews says would exceed the $63.7 billion in operating income Nvidia booked in its latest quarter. The estimate is up 782.5% from a year earlier, with sales put at 195 trillion won. TSMC, in a separate print the same day, reported record third-quarter revenue as AI chip demand held.

### Top Story
Samsung Electronics estimated on Thursday that third-quarter operating profit reached 107.4 trillion won, or $80.2 billion (€71.5 billion), up from 89.49 trillion won in the previous quarter and 12.17 trillion won a year earlier. Euronews calculates that as a 782.5% year-on-year increase. If confirmed, Euronews says it would be the biggest quarterly operating profit ever reported by a technology company, ahead of the $63.7 billion Nvidia booked in its latest quarter, and the first time a South Korean company's quarterly operating profit had topped 100 trillion won. Analysts had expected 106.1 trillion won, according to LSEG. Sales are estimated at 195 trillion won, or $145.6 billion, up 127% year-on-year, implying an operating margin of about 55%. Euronews reports the company is selling into AI data centres buying high-bandwidth memory while tight supply also lifts DRAM and NAND prices. Full results are due on 29 October. Shares closed 2.42% lower at 262,000 won as investors took profits, and the KOSPI lost 2.62%. Source: [euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/08/samsung-flags-783-profit-jump-to-record-80bn-as-ai-chip-boom-also-lifts-tsmc-sales)

### Silicon
**HPE's next ProLiant generation is built on 6th Gen AMD EPYC:** AMD
AMD said it is powering the next generation of HPE ProLiant servers with 6th Gen AMD EPYC processors, describing the machines as built for the AI era. The post names the processor generation and the server family. It does not add a core count, process node, or ship date. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/AMD/status/2107822744691757478)

### Data Centres & Power
**TogetherAI downgraded in ClusterMAX over reliability:** Dylan Patel (SemiAnalysis)
Dylan Patel said TogetherAI was downgraded in ClusterMAX because of reliability and quality issues, and that more than one site had problems. He said Nebius downtime and reliability issues were much less, and that the question for any cloud is how much downtime and how often, not whether downtime exists at all. He also said SemiAnalysis did not ask Iren or any cloud for payment for coverage or rankings. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/dylan522p/status/2108009082406007264)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**TSMC's third-quarter revenue print beats its own dollar guidance:** Seeking Alpha
TSMC reported record third-quarter revenue of NT$1.49 trillion, which Seeking Alpha puts at $46.71 billion, up 50% year-on-year and above the LSEG SmartEstimate of NT$1.46 trillion. TradingKey's tally from monthly prints is about NT$1.494 trillion, or about $46.8 billion, above the company's prior third-quarter dollar guidance of $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion. September consolidated revenue was NT$511.86 billion, about $16.07 billion, up 54.6% from September 2025 and down 0.6% from August. January through September revenue totalled NT$3,898.73 billion, about $122.42 billion, up 41.1% year-on-year. TradingKey says a Reuters survey of analysts expects third-quarter net profit of about NT$740.8 billion, up about 64% year-on-year; that figure is an estimate, not a company result. Prior company guidance for the quarter put gross margin at 65% to 67% and operating margin at 56% to 58%. The full report and earnings conference are set for 15 October. Source: [seekingalpha.com](https://seekingalpha.com/news/4651228-tsmcs-q3-revenue-jumps-50-yy-to-record-nt149t-beating-market-forecast) https://www.tradingkey.com/analysis/stocks/us-stocks/262205755-tsmc-q3-revenue-ai-demand-record-tradingkey, https://www.devdiscourse.com/article/business/3988867-tsmc-september-revenue-surges-546-yoy-to-usd-1607-billion-slips-marginally-month-on-month

**Rohm keeps wafers in-house and sends packages to Indian OSATs:** EE Times
Rohm Semiconductor is expanding outsourced assembly and test, starting with existing products and local Indian demand, while keeping wafer fabrication in-house. Managing director Makoto Terada told EE Times that Tata Electronics is assigned TOLL packages and Suchi Semicon is assigned TO-252. He said TOLL is widely used in the two-wheeler market and that the main customer base for TO-252 is more like four-wheeler. The first products will be power MOSFETs, legacy parts with a long production history inside Rohm, used to benchmark the new partners before any expansion toward global demand. Terada said the focus remains analog and power, and he did not indicate plans for advanced packaging in India at this stage. Both partners could eventually handle the same packages, he said, but that would depend on demand. Source: [eetimes.com](https://www.eetimes.com/rohm-semiconductor-expands-back-end-chip-manufacturing-outsourcing/)

### The Teardown: Why the Void Is Paid For Before It Is Seen
A hybrid-bonded stack does not fail like a wafer that can be scrapped at the lot. Value is already in the piece. Semiconductor Engineering describes advanced packaging as a place where cost accumulates layer by layer, component by component, and step by step, so that by the time chiplets, high-bandwidth memory stacks, or hybrid-bonded devices reach assembly, the manufacturer has already spent the material and the process time. An undetected defect at that point puts the larger assembly at risk, not a single die that never left the front end.

The defect list is not one optical problem. The same article names surface particles, cracks, embedded defects, microbump irregularities, and bonding voids, plus the need to measure bump height and surface profile. A particle on a bond pad and a void inside a bond are different failures, and a tool that only looks at the top surface will miss the second. High-sensitivity two-dimensional inspection is aimed at surface particles and pattern anomalies. High-speed infrared inspection is aimed at voids and embedded defects that stay hidden to a visible-light camera. Three-dimensional metrology is what measures microbump height and surface profile so the process engineer can tell a short bump from a dirty one.

That split is the mechanism. Hybrid bonding and fine-pitch bumps have pulled package tolerances toward the range historically associated with front-end fabrication, so the inspection problem is no longer "is the package cracked." It is whether a sidewall particle, a low-contrast defect, or a subsurface void is visible before the next layer is committed. Multi-angle illumination is described as a way to make sidewall and low-contrast defects show up when conventional brightfield or darkfield misses them. Electrical process control sits beside that optical stack: a later Semiconductor Engineering note on the same day frames the next process-control frontier as electrical as well as visual, because a bond that looks closed can still fail as a connection.

Sensitivity is constrained by the line, not by the microscope. If inspection throughput is too low, it becomes a bottleneck in a flow that is already capital-intensive. The design choice — catch the void with complementary optical, infrared, and height metrology before the stack is closed — stops being the right one when the only tools that can see the defect cannot keep up with the assembly rate, and the line either slows to the inspection step or ships assemblies whose internal bonds were never measured.

### On the Horizon
- TSMC's full third-quarter financial report and earnings conference are set for 15 October, with capacity utilization, gross margin, and demand guidance for the fourth quarter of 2026 and for 2027 on the list TradingKey says investors should watch.
- Samsung publishes full third-quarter results on 29 October, the date Euronews gives for the breakdown the Thursday estimate did not include.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **Twenty-four percent a year of data-centre power growth still leaves supply behind compute demand.**

**What You Need to Know:** McKinsey’s Global Energy Perspective 2026 puts data-centre electricity demand on a 24% compound annual path through 2030, and its most likely cases still have power supply below IT compute demand. The binding limit is how fast interconnection, turbines, transformers and construction can be delivered, not how many CPUs and GPUs are on order. Operators chasing speed are already turning to on-site engines, turbines, fuel cells and batteries.

### Top Story
McKinsey’s Global Energy Perspective 2026 says data-centre electricity demand could grow at a 24% compound annual rate through 2030, with the volume of computing that actually comes online set by power infrastructure rather than by chip orders alone. Sam DeFabrizio, a partner at McKinsey, told Data Center Knowledge: “From now to 2030, our most likely scenarios all have power supply lower than IT compute demand.” The projection mixes monthly tracking of CPU and GPU purchase commitments and hyperscaler capital-spending announcements with a delivery test: interconnection approvals, permitting, moratoriums, transformer lead times, turbines, reciprocating engines, fuel cells, and engineering, procurement and construction capacity. DeFabrizio said more construction and turbine manufacturing capacity, plus faster interconnection approvals and permitting, could let supply grow faster than the baseline; limited construction capacity or stronger efficiency gains — from models, from the buildings, or from shifting when workloads draw power — could pull electricity demand below it. The report’s wider point is that inexpensive generation cannot carry electrification unless transmission, storage and reliable capacity are ready to deliver it. Developers looking for faster power are turning to gas engines and turbines, fuel cells and battery storage. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/energy-power-supply/data-center-power-demand-to-grow-24-annually-by-2030-mckinsey)

### Silicon
**OpenAI selects AMD EPYC Turin CPUs to host Jalapeño: AMD**
AMD said OpenAI selected AMD EPYC “Turin” CPUs to host its Jalapeño AI ASIC deployment. The post, pointing to Tom’s Hardware, gives the reasons OpenAI’s team shared: platform strength, partner experience, and cutting unnecessary risk. This is a reported host-CPU selection for an ASIC deployment, not a merchant accelerator launch. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/AMD/status/2107514025323954628)

**Elastic Cloud adds Arm-based Azure Cobalt instances: Arm**
Arm said Elastic Cloud is adding compute-optimized instances on Arm-based Microsoft Azure Cobalt for compute-intensive search workloads. Elastic reports up to 44% better price-performance with its CPU Optimized Arm profile. The figure is Elastic’s reported price-performance for that profile, not a training-cluster benchmark. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/Arm/status/2107613394299662828)

**Gigabyte NVIDIA DGX Station, Grace beside Blackwell Ultra: ServeTheHome**
ServeTheHome published a hands-on, almost 10,000 words, on the Gigabyte NVIDIA DGX Station that brings an NVIDIA GB300-class system deskside. The piece’s network finding is that the NVIDIA Grace CPU and Blackwell Ultra have very different network connectivity. The write-up is a test of a deskside system, not a new NVIDIA platform announcement. Source: [servethehome.com](https://www.servethehome.com/gigabyte-w775-v10-l01-hands-on-bringing-nvidia-gb300-deskside/)

### Data Centres & Power
**EMEA build shifts past FLAP-D, and delivery is the test: Data Center Knowledge**

> **A reported six-point-nine-billion-dollar Huawei licence is not Qualcomm's deal, killing the LogicFolding claim.**

**What You Need to Know:** Qualcomm says a reported six-point-nine-billion-dollar Huawei licence is not its deal, and that LogicFolding is not part of the agreement. Uptime Institute's 2026 outage analysis puts UPS failures at 39 percent of power-related incidents. TrendForce expects TSMC mature-process prices to rise about 3 to 10 percent from January next year.

### Top Story
Qualcomm Licenses Huawei's LogicFolding, 5G, and Other Technologies: TechPowerUp
TechPowerUp reported a Qualcomm–Huawei licence estimated at $6.9 billion and, citing Bloomberg, tied it to Huawei's LogicFolding design. That initial account described two-sheet vertical stacking, a 55 percent transistor-density increase, and a 41 percent power-efficiency boost, framed as a way around sanctions and manufacturing limits. At 06:30 UTC on October 6, Qualcomm said the companies entered a multi-year, broad patent cross-licence across a range of technology fields. Terms are confidential. Qualcomm said reports that it is a net payor are incorrect, and that assertions the agreement is related to LogicFold are not accurate. Separately, Qualcomm has agreed to purchase certain Huawei non-cellular U.S. patents across multiple technology areas. Semiconductor Engineering's October 6 library add lists a HUST, PolyU, UC Santa Barbara, and National University of Singapore paper on low-contact-resistance ballistic p-type transistors in oxygen-doped WSe₂ monolayers. UC Santa Cruz contributed a design-space study of backside clock meshes for 2 nm GAAFET backside power delivery. Syracuse University, FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg, and TU Dresden added RAPID, on row-parallel arithmetic processing in DRAM. ### Data Centres & Power
**The UPS Is Uninterruptible by Design. Its Future Is Not.: Data Center Knowledge**
Data Center Knowledge reports that rack-level batteries, battery energy storage systems, and solid-state transformers are reopening where a UPS sits in the data-centre power train. Uptime Institute's Annual Outage Analysis 2026 found power-related issues behind more than one in five IT service outages over the past three years. Inside those power incidents, UPS failures led at 39 percent, ahead of transfer-switch failures at 34 percent and generator failures at 28 percent. The same research calls lithium-ion UPS batteries a clear contributing factor in a gradual rise in major data-centre fires, and notes the rise may partly track rapid facility build-out rather than battery chemistry alone. Hyperscale operators had already moved to Open Compute Project direct-current designs with distributed or rack-level UPS, including battery backup units, beside or instead of a centralized UPS. Higher-voltage direct current in AI factories, including 800 V DC, plus sidecar power cabinets, extends that distributed pattern toward extreme rack density. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/uptime/the-ups-is-uninterruptible-by-design-its-future-is-not-)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**TSMC Foundry Prices Expected to Rise Up to 10% Next Year, Signaling Domino Effect Across Fabless Industry: BigGo**
TrendForce says TSMC is planning to raise mature-process prices by about 3 to 10 percent starting January next year, BigGo reports. TSMC has reportedly decided on an additional 6 to 8 percent increase on 2 nm wafer prices in the first quarter of next year, citing manufacturing costs and electricity expenses. Individual customers have already seen increases of 10 to 20 percent in their pricing. Suppliers of power-management ICs, display-driver ICs, and microcontrollers are considering product-price rises of 5 percent to double-digit levels between late this year and early next year. SMIC has already raised prices on some demand-concentrated capacity for wafers produced from the third quarter; its second-quarter average wafer selling price rose 5.7 percent quarter over quarter, and utilization reached 93.7 percent. Some customers are pulling orders forward, citing capacity risk from Middle East conflict concerns and growing AI demand. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/ec2ae28d-b4ef-4b2e-ad4a-0b717dea689c)

**TSMC expansion pushes Da Yi Cheng Technology's orders over NT$10 billion, visibility through 2028: DigiTimes**
TSMC's expansion has pushed Da Yi Cheng Technology's orders over NT$10 billion, DigiTimes reports. Order visibility runs through 2028. Source: [digitimes.com](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20261006VL205/tsmc-2028-expansion-fab-equipment.html)

### The Teardown: Why the Cell Loses a Track When p Sits on n
A standard-cell track is a wiring lane that sets how tall the cell is. Gate-all-around nanosheet transistors, in imec's roadmap as published by Semiconductor Engineering, scale through the A10 logic generation and there enable 5.5-track cells. From the A7 node, imec says industry may move to a complementary FET: pMOS stacked on nMOS, so the two polarities stop sitting side by side and the cell can drop to 4.5 tracks and below. Push that stack further and the same roadmap puts cells at 3 tracks, which imec says can carry classical CMOS logic out to at least the A3 node. The height cut is not free silicon. Contacts, gates, and power still have to reach the buried device, which is why imec's design-technology work treats a backside contact and a gate stack that can set more than one threshold voltage as CFET-specific modules. Part 2 of that work, the piece dated for this window, adds a sequential-CFET cell that can be built as split-gate or common-gate. Split-gate keeps the two devices independently controllable, which logic and SRAM both need; common-gate is the tighter option when the pair should switch together. The SRAM result in that study is a 5-track-plus-one CFET bit cell. A second study in the same article works on back-end-of-line routability, because a shorter cell only helps if the wires above it can still escape. At A7, imec also leaves another path open: CMOS 2.0, partitioning a system-on-chip into heterogeneous tiers and stitching them with 3D interconnects, with power from the front or the back if nanosheets are pushed instead. The stacked cell stops being the right next step when the buried device cannot get an independent gate and a backside contact without giving the track height back to extra routing.

### On the Horizon
- TSMC's planned mature-process price increases start in January next year, in TrendForce's account via BigGo.
- An additional 6 to 8 percent on 2 nm wafer prices is set for the first quarter of next year, on the same reporting.

The system is based on the NVIDIA DGX Spark platform and is described as the same petaflop-scale architecture as the 128 GB configuration. At this year’s TSMC OIP conference, SK Hynix laid out a pipeline spanning high-bandwidth memory, server DRAM and solid-state drives, and took a second consecutive Partner of the Year award, with cooperation on HBM5 and CoWoS. The report says SK Hynix commands roughly 50 percent of global HBM revenue and is already negotiating volumes and pricing for 2027. Media reports have floated a Nasdaq listing for U.S. subsidiary Solidigm; management has stated that no capital plan for the subsidiary has been decided, and that any financing would first be assessed for its impact on existing shareholders and long-term corporate value. Source: [ad-hoc-news.de](https://www.ad-hoc-news.de/boerse/news/unternehmensnachrichten/sk-hynix-balances-ai-memory-roadmap-against-solidigm-financing-questions/70229405)

**SEC Co. Supplies HBM Inspection Equipment to Micron; Samsung, SK Inline Orders Imminent:** Biggo
Biggo reports that SEC Co. has supplied HBM inspection equipment to Micron. The same item describes inline orders from Samsung and SK as imminent. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/4be6a91b-ef72-4cc1-b609-b22f13690a99)

### The Teardown: Four Supplies for Eight Slots
A six-U chassis that holds eight full accelerators is a power problem before it is a compute problem. INNO3D’s announced AGS-6220V2, in TechPowerUp’s item on the product notice, pairs dual Intel Xeon 5th Gen Scalable processors and up to 32 DDR5 RDIMMs with eight PCIe Gen 5 x16 slots for NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. It feeds that stack from four 2700 W redundant Titanium power supplies.

The slot and the supply do different jobs. A PCIe Gen 5 x16 link is the attachment for data and for a limited amount of slot power. A server GPU at a sustained training or high-batch inference load does not live on that slot budget. Board power has to come from the chassis rails. Eight of those boards in six U put the rails, the bus bars and the converters in the same short column of air as the GPUs, so the supply count is as much a specification as the slot count.

Titanium, on the 80 Plus ladder, is the efficiency band in which the supply turns the least of each incoming watt into heat in its own magnetics and switches. Six U leaves no spare volume for a lazy converter. Redundant, on a four-supply set, means the nameplate is not the continuous budget: the chassis is built so one module can drop and the others still hold the rail. The notice lists four 2700 W supplies, eight GPU slots, two processors and up to 32 DIMMs, and it does not assign a wattage to each GPU. The nameplate is shared headroom and a spare, not a per-chip rating.

The tradeoff flips when the GPUs are not the load and the rack feed is already full. Extra Titanium modules then buy a hot-swap and a cleaner efficiency curve, not another accelerator. They also take airflow and rear cable space a denser tray would have given to another GPU. On a light inference or visualization node, the spare supply is insurance. On a fully loaded eight-GPU box sitting on a constrained rack circuit, those four modules are what let a supply be serviced without dropping the rail, and they are why a ninth card does not fit the power story. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/353391/inno3d-announces-6u-rtx-pro-6000bse-gpu-server)

### Silicon
**OpenAI says its own models optimised Astra Ultrafast's inference on Nvidia GPUs: MIXED Reality News**
OpenAI says its own models tuned the inference software serving GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast on Nvidia GPUs, a step past the earlier claim that the fast tier runs on Blackwell. ### Supply Chain & Policy
**This Under-the-Radar Supplier Could Be Nvidia's Secret Weapon: The Globe and Mail**
The Globe and Mail reports that high-bandwidth memory is packaged with AI chips such as Nvidia GPUs, stacked beside the GPU die, because without it the processors wait on data and power use climbs. It names three HBM makers — Samsung, Micron and SK Hynix — and says new clean-room space takes years to build. HBM takes upwards of three times the wafer capacity of conventional DRAM. Those memory makers are also competing with logic chipmakers for extreme-ultraviolet lithography tools, and ASML is the only company that makes those machines. The same piece reports SK Hynix as Nvidia’s primary HBM supplier, with a large supply agreement locking in volume for the GPU maker. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/investing/markets/stocks/ASML-Q/pressreleases/4948788/this-under-the-radar-supplier-could-be-nvidia-s-secret-weapon/)

**ASML vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company: The Globe and Mail**
The Globe and Mail reports that, in the three months ending September 25, 2026, ASML formally announced a collaborative initiative with TSMC to move toward large-format photomasks. The same account says ASML is navigating broader demand delays affecting ongoing global data-centre construction. The photomask step is an announced process collaboration; the construction delays are a reported condition, not a named site cancellation. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/investing/markets/stocks/TSM-N/pressreleases/4944927/asml-vs-taiwan-semiconductor-manufacturing-company-what-revenue-trends-tell-investors-about-these-companies-tied-to-artificial-intelligence/)

### The Teardown: When a Wafer Chain Goes Offline
A wafer-scale part is sold as one computer the size of a wafer. Chaining is the next claim: stitch many of those wafers into one logical machine so a single job can see all of them. Dylan Patel of SemiAnalysis, writing on X on October 4, pushed back on a reading that treats such a chain as delivered and fully utilized. His point was narrow and physical: chaining dozens and dozens of wafers together brings quite a few offline and utilization issues.

The mechanism is a failure domain, not a brochure diagram. Each wafer is its own yield lottery. A conventional packaged chip throws out the bad die and ships the good ones. A wafer that is the product cannot do that as cleanly. Defects, a dead link, a power fault or a cooling fault take that wafer out of the chain. Once wafers are wired as one machine, the job scheduler either shrinks the job to the wafers still answering or waits on the missing slice. Waiting is idle silicon that still occupies power, network ports and floor space. Shrinking the job means the nameplate — dozens and dozens of wafers — is not the capacity a customer can book every hour.

Utilization then splits in two. Delivery utilization asks whether every wafer in the purchase order is on the floor and powered. Online utilization asks whether those wafers are in the same chain at the same time, with links healthy enough to pass traffic. A chain multiplies the second problem. One offline wafer does not merely subtract one wafer’s compute. It can force a rebalance across the remaining chain, and a second fault in another wafer can split the machine into islands that cannot see one another. Spares help only if they are already cabled, already cooled and already in the address map. A spare in a crate is not a spare in a chain.

That is why “all delivered and fully utilized” is a stronger claim than “wafers shipped.” Shipment counts wafers that left the dock. A chained system counts wafers that are up, linked and scheduled together. Patel’s objection is that the second number is the one that pays for the power and the building, and chaining dozens and dozens of wafers makes that second number harder to hold. The tradeoff flips when the job can be cut into pieces smaller than the chain, so one offline wafer costs one wafer, not a stall of the whole machine. Until the software can do that, the chain’s headline size and its usable size are different machines.

### On the Horizon

Source: [semiconductor-digest.com](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/emd-electronics-opens-new-rd-facility-in-wisconsin/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=emd-electronics-opens-new-rd-facility-in-wisconsin)

In an International Manufacturing Day post, Micron listed new fabs in Idaho and New York, a modernized plant in Virginia, manufacturing and advanced packaging investment in Singapore, a cleanroom expansion in Japan, expanded operations in Taiwan, and India’s first assembly and test facility in Sanand. The post is a company statement of that footprint, not a new site groundbreaking dated today. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/MicronTech/status/2106109129920262366)

### The Teardown: One Cache Die, or Two
A 64 MB SRAM die bonded on top of a compute chiplet is the mechanism in AMD’s 3D V-Cache. The stack puts extra last-level memory on the vertical path, so a core that keeps hitting the same working set can stay on the package instead of going out to DRAM. The bond is also a lid. The chiplet under the cache die has to shed heat through that extra silicon and live with the voltage the stack will accept, and that is what shows up as a lower boost clock when both chiplets are covered.

TechPowerUp’s write-up of a Chiphell post is the measurement set. An engineering sample of the never-released Ryzen 9 5900X3D, code 100-000000652, reports 128 MB of L3, split as 96 MB on one CCD and 32 MB on the other. Only one of the two six-core chiplets carries the 64 MB stack. CPU-Z screenshots from the owner show the part around 4.7 GHz with a 105 W TDP. The dual-stack 5900X3D prototypes AMD showed Gamers Nexus in 2023 had cache on both CCDs, 192 MB in total, and topped out at a 4.4 GHz boost. The sample would not boot on current BIOS versions and started only with older firmware carrying SMU 56.70.0. AMD has not confirmed the part.

Retail Zen 3 X3D began with the eight-core Ryzen 7 5800X3D in 2022 and never included a dual-CCD chip. The single-stack layout is the one AMD later used for Ryzen 9 X3D chips on AM5, before the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 Dual Edition put cache on both chiplets this year. Cover both chiplets and the capacity figure is the one that moves. Leave one CCD bare and the clock figure is the one that moves.

> **A 0.0094-square-micrometre cell, 52.7 percent smaller than N3, is Lam's path past 10 angstroms.**

**What You Need to Know:** Lam Research's digital-twin model of a self-aligned CFET produced a 0.0094-square-micrometre 6T SRAM cell, 52.7 percent smaller than N3, with at least a 10-nanometre overlay window, as a proposal to push CMOS below 10 angstroms. Nvidia put agent controls on BlueField-4, AMD Instinct halved Character.ai's cost per token on the same footprint, and Korea's chip exports hit 60 billion dollars in September. Developers are buying batteries and substations, while a reported AI factory build sits near 60 million dollars.

### Top Story
Semiconductor Engineering reports that Lam Research has proposed a self-aligned CFET architecture meant to extend CMOS scaling below 10 angstroms. Digital-twin modeling produced a 6T SRAM bit cell of 0.0094 square micrometres, 52.7 percent smaller than an N3 bit cell. The model keeps at least a 10-nanometre overlay window across critical contact layers. The result is a proposed architecture and a modeled cell, not a process in volume production. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-158/)

### Silicon

**AMD Instinct GPUs Double Character.ai Inference Throughput: AMD**
AMD says Character.ai, running on AMD Instinct GPUs at DigitalOcean, doubled production inference throughput and cut cost per token by 50 percent. The same compute footprint is what AMD says now holds that higher throughput. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/AMD/status/2105708098388189407)

### Data Centres & Power
**From Opposition to Buy-In: Data Center Knowledge**
Data Center Knowledge reports that sessions at Data Center World Power in Dallas, September 21–23, dealt with community opposition to data centers over water, power, and noise, and with bans and moratoria. Power availability and possible electricity rate hikes are among the biggest worries, and in some regions data centers are being blamed for higher rates. Many developers are willing to fund the upgrades their projects need; some have paid for entire battery energy storage systems that serve both the grid and the data center. Others are contributing to transmission upgrades or buying transformers, substations, and other power electronics so those costs are not passed to ratepayers, and some grid planners and utilities are formalizing such arrangements as standard practice. Diane Sullivan, chief development officer of Hecate Energy, a Chicago-based developer of utility-scale energy parks, tied part of the backlash to non-disclosure agreements with city officials and to projects developed under the radar, and said AI data centers are now large enough that engaging the community upfront is in the developer's long-term interest. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-site-selection/from-opposition-to-buy-in-tactics-for-data-center-developers)

**NVIDIA GPUs Help AI Factories Get The Most Tokens Per Megawatt: Quantum Zeitgeist**
Quantum Zeitgeist reports that each AI factory now costs approximately 60 million dollars to build, and that operators are focused on return. NVIDIA is engineering those factories for the highest throughput per megawatt; tokens per second per megawatt govern revenue generation. The Vera Rubin NVL72 is the system named for that earning capacity, with gains attributed to codesign across models, workloads, software, compute, networking, and memory. The NVIDIA A100, shipped in 2020, is still in commercial service six years later. CUDA-X libraries are how NVIDIA says a factory can run any accelerated workload, not only AI, and a SemiAnalysis AgentX analysis indicates that demand for compute does not diminish as each hardware generation becomes more efficient. Source: [quantumzeitgeist.com](https://quantumzeitgeist.com/nvidia-gpus-help-factories-get/)

### Supply Chain & Policy

**JCET Group Partners with Wuxi on 2.5D Packaging: DIGITIMES**
DIGITIMES reports that JCET Group signed an agreement on September 29 for a high-end advanced packaging and testing project in Wuxi, Jiangsu Province. The project is to advance 2.5D advanced packaging facilities. Source: [digitimes.com](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20261002VL207/jcet-packaging-high-end-manufacturing-silicon.html)

### The Teardown: Why a New Node Is Still a Sliver of Wafer Revenue
In the second quarter of 2026, 2-nanometre product accounted for 3 percent of TSMC wafer revenue, Spherical Insights reports, against 33 percent for 5-nanometre wafers and 30 percent for 3-nanometre wafers. Revenue for the quarter was 40.2 billion dollars. A new node does not take the paycheck on announcement day. Three physical queues have to finish, and they finish on different clocks. Design teams must close libraries, memory compilers, and a tape-out on the new rules. The fab must install and qualify the lithography, etch, and deposition set before it can offer a monthly wafer start. Yield must rise until a good die costs less than staying on the prior node. Customers with masks, intellectual property, and package designs already qualified on the older nodes move only the chips that need the density or the power. The rest stays where yield is already known. A node can therefore be in production and still be a sliver of the income statement. Wafers on the newest node are shipping, and the two older nodes still hold most of what the foundry sold. The 40.2 billion dollars means that sliver is cut from a very large quarter, not from a pilot line. The tradeoff flips when good-die cost on the new node, at the volume a buyer can actually book, undercuts the older node on performance per watt or on the wafers per month that buyer can get. Until that slot is bookable, the revenue mix marks where the tools and the masks already sit.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **Sixty-nine kilovolts is now the cutoff for a foreign-equipment ban on the US grid.**

**What You Need to Know:** Sixty-nine kilovolts is now the cutoff for a foreign-equipment ban on the US grid, under an August 26 emergency order that can reach transformers, inverters and control systems. CoreWeave has put NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 into limited cloud availability, with Cognition reporting up to 4.8 times the token throughput per GPU of a GB200 NVL72 on its own test. A Taiwanese press report adds a six-fab Dallas outline to talk of a Texas TSMC campus, still without a board approval.

### Top Story
On August 26, 2026, President Trump signed an executive order declaring a national emergency to ban or restrict acquisition and installation of high-risk foreign-produced equipment in the US electric grid, citing hidden cybersecurity vulnerabilities, malware and remote-access risk. It covers equipment, hardware, software and firmware used in generation, transmission or control facilities operating at 69 kilovolts or above, including large transformers, grid-tied inverters, circuit breakers, battery energy storage systems, SCADA software and industrial control systems. Equipment used only in local low-voltage distribution falls outside it, including standard residential solar inverters and commercial distribution below 69 kilovolts. A covered foreign entity is any company owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction of a foreign adversary, including arms-embargo countries such as Russia, Iran and North Korea, with China described as the real power-sector concern, and a US or European manufacturer can still be caught if critical chips, communications modules or internal software come from a covered jurisdiction. Transactions after August 26, 2026 can be restricted, the Secretary of Energy can require earlier installs to be monitored, disconnected, replaced or removed, and US utilities are already pausing procurement tied to foreign-linked supply chains. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/us-executive-order-on-energy-grid-supply-chain-security/)

### Silicon
**CoreWeave Puts Vera Rubin NVL72 Into Limited Availability: Techgenyz**
After racks were already reported shipping, CoreWeave said on September 30 that NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 is in limited availability on CoreWeave Cloud, with Cognition the first customer running production workloads. On SWE-2 inference drawn from a sampled subset of FrontierCode tasks, Cognition measured up to 4.8 times higher total token throughput per GPU than a GB200 NVL72 baseline at matched interactivity. Cognition’s engineers took those figures on CoreWeave infrastructure, and the report says independent third-party verification has not yet appeared. In CoreWeave testing, the Vera CPU produced more than 3 times faster agent-sandbox startup than an unnamed alternative x86 CPU. The same account states that higher token throughput is not a higher task-success rate. Source: [techgenyz.com](https://techgenyz.com/cognition-running-devin-workloads-nvidia-vera-rubin/)

### Data Centres & Power
**Can Data Center Design Choices Change Public Acceptance?: Data Center Knowledge**
Operators are using biomimicry, community co-design and brownfield redevelopment to cut the visual impact of data centers and ease local objections that already include noise, energy and water. Microsoft first used biomimicry at a Noord-Holland site in 2022, planting 150 native trees and more than 2,000 square meters, about 21,500 square feet, of shrubs and grasses. The company says it has since expanded the practice to more than 20 sites across the US and Europe. Director of global land strategy Kaitlin Chuzi told Data Center Knowledge that the work starts from how the local ecosystem functions, combining ecological research with community input to shape land, water and restoration plans. The Virginia-based Piedmont Environmental Council, cited in the same report, describes proposed county hyperscale sites as massive, windowless concrete buildings that can bring noise, substations and transmission lines, and that sit out of scale with existing communities. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/sustainability/can-data-center-design-choices-change-public-acceptance-)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**UDN Adds a Six-Fab Dallas Outline to the Texas Talk: TechPowerUp**
Taiwan’s Economic Daily News, citing semiconductor equipment industry sources, reports that TSMC is planning a second US manufacturing campus in Texas, separate from Arizona, with six advanced fabs and Dallas the most likely location. UDN estimates the investment could exceed the $265 billion committed to Arizona, on the view that the new fabs would probably use more advanced nodes. Reuters, as cited in that report, says TSMC is evaluating a potential Texas investment, plans are not finalized, and one source said it would come on top of the Arizona commitment. TSMC had not commented when the report went out, has not asked suppliers to prepare, and the board has not signed off. UDN says the Arizona site still faces power and labor shortages while it sorts out its water supply, after TSMC added another $100 billion to those Arizona plans in July, and points to a renewed tariff threat of up to 200 percent for chipmakers that do not produce in the US. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/353281/tsmc-reportedly-evaluating-texas-expansion-besides-usd-265-billion-arizona-plan)

### The Teardown: Why a Limb Log Wears Out Flash
A joint that has to keep the last safe pose does not lose that pose in the neural network. It loses it in the log. Take the write path apart at the limb microcontroller, not at the vision computer. Semiconductor Engineering describes a zonal machine: a central compute core runs vision, model execution and motion planning, and a time-sensitive network pushes commands to microcontrollers in the limbs, the joint actuators and the battery system. Those edge controllers are picked for deterministic low latency and for power-loss persistence, so a brownout does not bring a joint back in an unknown state. The same piece says logging motor torque, velocity and limb position at sampling rates above 10 kilohertz can exceed the endurance of conventional non-volatile memory. The wear mechanism is block erase. Embedded flash does not rewrite a single sample in place. It erases a whole block, and a shift-long sample stream never pauses long enough for that block to be written once and left alone. Small log lines therefore become repeated erases. That is write amplification, and it spends the cell’s life on bookkeeping rather than on the sensor count. Memory sized for the vision workload does not stand in. The article separates high-bandwidth memory, used for large networks on the central processor, from latency-optimized memory on the distributed controllers. A wide inference path does not hold the last torque command through a power cut beside the motor driver. Goldman Sachs figures cited there put annual humanoid shipments at fewer than 15,000 units in 2025 and possibly more than 6 million by 2035. Endurance that looks acceptable on a demo stand is a fleet problem at the second figure. The tradeoff flips when logging stops being a continuous stream and becomes a checkpoint on a fault or a mode change. Block erases then fall back inside what ordinary flash is built to survive, and the high-endurance part on the limb is no longer what limits the design.

### On the Horizon
: the Department of Energy is due to publish implementing rules for the grid-equipment order, as a prohibited-entity list, a pre-qualified vendor list, or both.
 p.m. PT: AMD chair and CEO Lisa Su gives the OCP Global Summit opening keynote, “Building the Next Era of AI Infrastructure.”

**E-Series GPU IP: The First Step Towards Converged Acceleration: Semiconductor Engineering**

**Intel "Nova Lake" Launch Nears as Platform Passes USB4 and PCIe 5.0 Compliance Testing: TechPowerUp**
TechPowerUp reports that Intel's Core Ultra 400-series Nova Lake CPUs are nearing launch after the platform passed USB and PCIe compliance testing, which the outlet treats as confirmation that advertised specifications are working. In August, device IDs D461, D465, and D467-D46A certified a PCIe 5.0 x16 root complex; TechPowerUp says those IDs are likely Nova Lake-S CPUs or a mobile variant. The outlet calls compliance verification the final stage a platform usually clears before launch is finalized. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/353240/intel-nova-lake-launch-nears-as-platform-passes-usb4-and-pcie-5-0-compliance-testing)

**PCIe 8.0 Over UCIe 3.0: Bringing A Proven Protocol Into The Chiplet Era: Semiconductor Engineering**
Semiconductor Engineering describes PCIe 8.0 carried over UCIe 3.0 as a way to keep a familiar protocol when a design splits across chiplets. UCIe standardizes die-to-die communication inside a package. That path lets PCIe traffic cross chiplet boundaries with interoperability over the standardized interconnect. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/pcie-8-0-over-ucie-3-0-bringing-a-proven-rrotocol-into-the-chiplet-era/)

### Data Centres & Power
**Digital Realty Plans Cable Landing Station at Los Angeles Data Center: Data Center Knowledge**
Digital Realty has announced plans for a cable landing station at a Los Angeles data center. The company describes it as its first turnkey cable landing station, designed to bring subsea capacity directly into an established data center and interconnection environment. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/cables/digital-realty-plans-cable-landing-station-at-los-angeles-data-center)

**MagPro launches AeroLev 1850 to advance water-smart cooling for AI data centers: Data Center Dynamics**
MagPro has launched the AeroLev 1850, which the company says eliminates evaporative cooling water. Data Center Dynamics reports that dropping that water use removes a significant operational constraint for data centers in arid and water-stressed regions. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/product-news/magpro-launches-aerolev-1850-to-advance-water-smart-cooling-for-ai-data-centers/)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**Da-Li Development spends nearly NT$600 million on Phoenix office property to tap TSMC supply chain opportunities: Biggo**
Da-Li Development is spending nearly NT$600 million on office property in Phoenix. The purchase is aimed at opportunities in the TSMC supply chain. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/ba6ece1d-0ef1-49b8-827e-6a2913ce4727)

### The Teardown: Moving the job instead of the megawatt
Carbon intensity on a data-centre feeder is an hourly quantity, not a nameplate on the building. Take the flexible queue apart and the lever is which work is allowed to wait. Data Center Knowledge describes carbon-aware computing as scheduling compute-intensive but time-flexible tasks when grid carbon intensity is lower, or when on-site renewable or stored energy is available. The tasks it names are data backups, batch analytics, AI model training, report generation, and non-urgent patching. The comparison is emissions from running the workload at one time or one place versus another, then the option that cuts emissions inside the rules the operator already has.

Operators have to know which jobs can move without breaking service-level agreements, latency requirements, data-residency constraints, or change-control policies. A backup, a batch analytics pass, a training run, a report, or a non-urgent patch might move. The grid side of that comparison moves because generation moves. Solar production peaks in daylight. Wind output varies by season and by hour. Some regions sit on geothermal, hydro, or nuclear baseload. Demand, transmission constraints, and market dispatch then change what is actually serving the next kilowatt-hour, so the emissions intensity of that kilowatt-hour can swing significantly inside a single day.

The policy that falls out of the comparison is a filter on incremental demand. Flexible load is pointed at cleaner windows so it does not force extra consumption in higher-emitting hours. Data Center Knowledge puts that result next to long-term renewable procurement and efficiency programs: a practical path to lower Scope 2 emissions, and a way to show progress toward 24/7 carbon-free energy objectives while regulatory expectations and stakeholder scrutiny of data-centre electricity demand keep rising. The tradeoff flips the moment a cleaner hour would breach an SLA, a latency bound, a residency rule, or a change window. The job stays on the dirtier hour, and the carbon accounting follows the promise the service already made.

### On the Horizon
- Next year, Chosun Ilbo reports, HBM is set to consume 30 percent of global DRAM wafer capacity.

### The Teardown: When the Rack's Coolant Has to Change
Heat leaves the rack, or the accelerators throttle. Data Center Knowledge, citing Bill Kleyman, reports AI workloads driving typical rack densities from roughly 10–30 kilowatts into 80–150 kilowatts, with advanced deployments approaching 1 megawatt per rack.

Air cooling is a volume problem. Fans push room air across a heatsink; the air carries heat to a coil elsewhere in the building. The ceiling is flow. More flow means more pressure drop through the cabinet, more risk that hot-aisle air comes back to the inlet, and a point where the electrical feed and the airflow fail together. Another card in that rack then adds temperature, not useful work.

Liquid cooling changes the carrier, not the need to reject the heat. A pump moves water or a dielectric across a cold plate, or the board sits in a bath, and a coolant distribution unit hands the load to the building loop. A small liquid flow moves heat that would have required a large air flow. Kleyman tied that shift to AFCOM's State of the Data Center 2026 survey: 69 percent of respondents expect rack density to increase like nothing seen in the past, and liquid-cooling adoption is showing 36 percent growth.

The parts in the rack show why the old air budget breaks. Kleyman said a standard rack can hold six Nvidia DGX-class systems, each built around eight H100 accelerators, with individual accelerator cards costing up to $40,000. That population does not fit a 10–30 kilowatt cabinet as a full set. It starts to fit between 80 and 150 kilowatts. Near 1 megawatt per rack, the design is busbar plus coolant loop, not a deeper air plenum.

The tradeoff flips inside the old 10–30 kilowatt band. Pumps and plates then add leak paths without buying accelerators the air system could already feed. Once a deployment approaches 1 megawatt per rack, staying on air means leaving some of those $40,000 cards out, or asking the hall for airflow it cannot move.

**Xcena MX1 combines DDR5, SSDs and RISC-V cores over CXL:** Xcena’s MX1 uses CXL to push compute into memory. The design combines DDR5, SSDs and RISC-V cores. Data movement is reduced to address memory bottlenecks in AI workloads. Programmability is eased by the architecture. The RISC-V cores sit directly alongside the memory arrays. Local reductions and filtering occur before data crosses the host PCIe bus. Each CXL-attached module therefore cuts traffic volume. The SSDs serve as a slower but larger tier. ### The Teardown: CXL Memory Pooling in the MX1
Take it apart and the MX1 places RISC-V cores directly alongside DDR5 and SSD arrays connected through CXL links. This layout lets the cores perform local reductions and filtering before any data crosses the host PCIe bus. Each CXL-attached module therefore cuts the volume of traffic that would otherwise traverse the narrower host interface. The design also lets the SSDs serve as a slower but larger tier that the RISC-V cores can address without first staging everything in host DRAM. When the working set fits inside the pooled DDR5, latency stays comparable to local memory; once the set spills to the SSD tier, bandwidth drops but capacity scales without adding more host sockets. The tradeoff flips when the ratio of compute to data movement exceeds the CXL link rate, at which point the added cores no longer offset the extra hop.

### The Teardown: Qualifying a Packaging Tool Beside the Vendor
An advanced packaging tool is not qualified when it is unpacked. It is qualified when bond alignment, bond force, and the heat steps around a logic die and a memory stack have been run on the customer's flow, with the customer's limits deciding pass or fail. A vendor's own demonstration line cannot finish that job, because the warpage, the stack, and the test limits belong to the customer. That is why a verification center is built as a shared floor, not as another brochure lab.

Taiwan Economic Daily News, reported by Asiae, says the groundbreaking for the Kaohsiung Baifu Industrial Park was held on September 21. TSMC, the Ministry of Economic Affairs, and the Kaohsiung city government are starting what the report calls Taiwan's first advanced semiconductor equipment and materials verification center. The plan puts TSMC's advanced packaging verification center, a talent development center, and exclusive factories for partner companies on one site. Asiae reports that more than 20 suppliers are already planning to move in, and that TSMC is committed to supporting that move-in.

The mechanism is proximity. A process tweak on a bonder can be tried, measured, and rejected beside the customer's verification team, instead of being discovered after the tool has been dropped into a hall that is already running volume. Scrap at that stage is not a blank wafer. It is a finished die joined to finished memory. Keeping the tool company and the packaging customer on one site is how that scrap is supposed to stay off the volume line.

Asiae says a standard factory is scheduled for completion in the second quarter of 2028, and that the verification laboratory and the talent development center are set to open in phases in the fourth quarter of the same year. The tradeoff flips if that shared lab arrives later than a tool slot on a line that already exists. Partners who cannot wait until 2028 will still qualify across separate sites. The September 21 groundbreaking starts construction of the loop.

### The Teardown: The Row CDU Still Sets the Hall
An in-row coolant distribution unit takes heat off a secondary loop at the end of the aisle, so the cold plate on the package is not the building heat exchanger. StorageReview reports Supermicro NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 racks now shipping with 1.8-megawatt in-row CDUs and a 1,152-GPU scalable unit. That 1.8 megawatts is the thermal duty the row exchanger is built to move continuously. The 1,152-GPU count is the failure domain: pumps, valves, manifolds, and power for that many accelerators sit behind one scalable-unit boundary, so a flow fault is a row event. A CDU at that rating is plant equipment. Quick-disconnects, heat exchangers, and redundant pumps have to be qualified as a mechanical system before the hall accepts the IT load. AMD, in a separate validation note, describes a double-wide rack at 8,000 pounds lifted onto a vibration test while Helios is checked for real-world handling. Liquid manifolds and a chassis that wide add mass; the shaker is how joints and connectors are shown to survive lift and floor vibration before coolant is trusted in the row. Pluang reports, which is the demand pulling these row designs into shipping racks rather than lab slides. Chip-level efficiency does not retire the row plant by itself. The tradeoff flips only when the GPU count inside the scalable unit drops, or when heat per GPU falls far enough that a smaller CDU can cover the same row. Until one of those two moves, pipes, pumps, and floor loading are sized to the 1.8-megawatt row and the 8,000-pound lift.

### Data Centres & Power
**Vertiv agrees to buy King Environmental Services: Data Center Dynamics**
Vertiv has agreed to acquire Ireland-based King Environmental Services, which provides fluid management, commissioning and load-testing for high-density, liquid-cooled data centers. The deal is meant to extend Vertiv’s thermal-management services into EMEA; the company already offers fluid management in North America. Last year Vertiv bought PurgeRite, another firm in the same work, for more than $1 billion. Chief executive Gio Albertazzi said that as computing density increases, cooling and power performance “will depend as much on execution in the field as on engineering and system design.” KES, founded in 2002 and headquartered near Dublin, serves customers across EMEA, and its site lists projects for Microsoft and Equinix. ### Supply Chain & Policy

Laminate capacity of 20 million square feet per year is scheduled online in January 2027. Build-up and prepreg capacity of 87 million square feet per year is scheduled online in November 2026. Source: [semiconductor-digest.com](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/accm-expands-us-manufacturing-capacity-across-four-advanced-materials-segments-for-ai-infrastructure/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=accm-expands-us-manufacturing-capacity-across-four-advanced-materials-segments-for-ai-infrastructure)

It also reports that TSMC partners are accelerating, and that China is doubling down on AI compute and memory. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-157/)

### The Teardown: Rack Mass Versus Rack Price
You take it apart at the floor plate, not at the silicon. A data-centre slab is rated for a point load and a uniform load, and the rack designer spends that allowance on busbar, manifold, cold plates and coolant until the frame is as heavy as the tile allows. The invoice is not part of that drawing. Dylan Patel wrote that a fully populated GB300 NVL72 weighs roughly 1,580 kilograms, that recent purchase orders put the rack at 5 million dollars, that the GB200 NVL72 was 4 million dollars, and that Vera Rubin NVL72 is already quoted at up to 8.8 million dollars at essentially the same rack mass. Those four figures sit on one chassis envelope. High-bandwidth memory, the CoWoS package that bonds it to the GPU, and the power stages that feed both add little mass and most of the price. Patel's point is that those three stay supply-limited, so dollars per kilogram rise while floor loading holds the kilogram count still. The unit you accept on the dock is the populated rack, which is why he prices the frame rather than the bare packages. A higher quote does not buy a heavier rack, and a heavier rack would not clear a slab already at its rating. The tradeoff flips when packaging allocation or feeder capacity, not steel, is what you lack: price can move inside a fixed tile, and the tile cannot grow to match the quote.

- Vertiv expects the King Environmental Services acquisition to close before the end of 2026.
- Applied Digital anticipates initial operations in August 2027 at Polaris Forge 3, a 300-megawatt critical IT load on 600 acres in an unnamed northern state, for the same US investment-grade hyperscaler previously signed for Delta Forge 1.

### Supply Chain & Policy
**Qualcomm sticks with TSMC for both 2nm Snapdragon flagships: Digitimes**
